title: Structural counterfactuals for macroeconomic regimes

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a structural macroeconomic model that credibly estimates how inflation, employment, and output would respond when monetary or fiscal policy follows a different rule. A policy rule describes how authorities respond to economic conditions, rather than just a single interest-rate or spending decision. The model would account for households and firms changing their expectations and behavior when they learn that the policy process has changed.

The central distinction is between policy-invariant primitives—the underlying features assumed to remain stable across the policies being compared—and decision rules that respond to the policy environment. The objective is not to hold every estimated parameter fixed. It is to identify stable mechanisms well enough to predict how behavior changes under a specified new regime, then expose those predictions to prospective evaluation. This describes a target capability; the supplied evidence does not establish that it has been achieved or conclusively establish its present-day absence.

significance.text: Conditional on credible structural identification and successful prospective validation, this capability would give central banks and treasuries a substantially stronger basis for comparing monetary and fiscal rules before adopting them. Accurate tracking of an existing regime does not establish that a model can evaluate a different one. The direct advance would be empirically defensible comparisons of alternative policy processes, including their implications for inflation and real activity.

Conditional downstream possibilities include better preparation for policy transitions, clearer comparisons of stabilization tradeoffs, and more informative communication about the uncertainty surrounding a proposed rule. These are potential benefits of the capability, not demonstrated outcomes. Its revolutionary significance would lie in making policy comparisons more reliable before decisions are taken.

A successful forecast through one realized transition would not, by itself, validate the policies that were never implemented. Nor would it prove that the model had identified invariant primitives or that authorities could reliably control the economy. The analogy to turning stabilization into engineering therefore exceeds what the proposed demonstration could establish: predictive performance, causal counterfactual validity, and dependable policy control are distinct achievements.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central scientific challenge is to distinguish stable structural mechanisms from behavioral relationships that depend on the policy process. Lucas's critique explains why decision rules estimated under one policy environment cannot generally be carried unchanged into another. A convincing solution must model how expectations and choices adjust to the new rule, including what agents know about the change and when they learn it.

An additional identification challenge is to distinguish a model that predicts a realized transition well from one that correctly represents the mechanisms needed to evaluate unobserved alternatives. Prospective forecasts supply valuable evidence, but they need complementary identification evidence and validation across different settings. The supplied materials do not demonstrate that this combined capability is available, and their limited coverage cannot establish a field-wide absence as of November 1, 2026.

Computational tractability is an enabling challenge rather than a substitute for identification. Fast solution of a heterogeneous-agent model does not establish that its expectations assumptions describe actual behavior or that its primitives remain stable across real policy changes. The retained computational paper explicitly separates its solution method from an empirically realistic account of human learning. Heterogeneous-agent modeling is one possible input to the target capability, not an established requirement for every solution.

The original research also raises the possibility that large shocks change price-setting frequencies and other relationships treated as fixed in small-shock models. That could be an additional modeling barrier, but the supplied review found no retained source text supporting this particular assertion. It remains an unverified consideration rather than an established explanation of the missing breakthrough.

current_state.text: Lucas's 1976 analysis established the conceptual problem: successful short-term forecasting by the major econometric models he examined did not establish their suitability for evaluating alternative policy rules, because decision rules respond to the policy process. His argument motivates structural policy evaluation; it does not establish that every subsequent model fails or that the target capability remains unavailable today. The supplied review had a full extraction of this paper, with interpretable OCR imperfections.

The supplied research presents the 2021–2022 inflation surge as a modern forecasting stress test. It attributes to Koch and Noureldin's May 12, 2023 IMF working paper world-average headline-inflation forecast errors of 1.7 percentage points in 2021 and 3.2 points in 2022, compared with approximately −0.1 point in 2010–2019. It also reports root-mean-square forecast errors respectively 2.5 and 5 times the 2010–2019 level. No source artifact or retained text from this paper was available in the supplied review, so these exact figures remain attributed research claims that could not be independently assessed there. That access limitation does not show that the figures are false. Forecast misses alone also do not identify their cause as a failure to model a policy-regime change.

The research attributes to Bernanke and Blanchard's June 2023 analysis the conclusion that most of the initial US pandemic-era inflation surge came from price shocks relative to wages, while tight labor markets contributed more persistently afterward. The supplied review had no retained artifact from this source and therefore could not verify that decomposition. As characterized in the research, it is an ex post explanation of the observed inflation path; such an explanation does not meet a test requiring forecasts committed before the transition.

A preliminary December 2025 paper by Yang, Wang, Schaab, and Moll reports substantial computational progress on heterogeneous-agent benchmarks. Its table gives average solution times across ten runs of 56.55 seconds for Krusell–Smith, 75.29 seconds for Huggett with aggregate shocks, and 199.53 seconds for HANK with aggregate shocks, using a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. These are reported benchmark computations, not prospective forecasts of actual economic regime changes.

The solver computes restricted perceptions equilibria rather than the models' rational-expectations equilibria. Its authors also state that their method is not an empirically realistic model of human learning. The review notes an author claim of some immunity to the Lucas critique, but that theoretical claim does not establish empirically identified invariant primitives or prospective real-world performance. The results support fast computation for the reported calibrated benchmarks; they do not establish that computation has ceased to be a barrier for every relevant model.

The computational evidence has specific coverage limits. The retained PDF extraction ends during page 45, limiting assessment of the remaining material. Both the retained landing page and PDF identify December 2025 version 1, with the landing page recording submission on December 21, 2025; they do not substantiate the separately mentioned August 2026 version date. No bounded freshness-search results were supplied. Consequently, this record describes dated achievements and evidence gaps rather than a comprehensive assessment of the field through November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: before a clearly defined policy-regime change, deposit the model, its conditional forecasts, uncertainty bands, and scoring rules. Define the old and new policy processes and account for when households, firms, and markets learn about the transition. Evaluate inflation and specified real-activity outcomes over the following two years. The two-year horizon is a proposed design choice, not an established scientific standard.
completion_criteria.label: Precommit forecasts before regime change for two-year outcome evaluation

completion_criteria.text: The proposed accuracy requirement is that errors remain within a pre-registered standard referenced to comparable forecasts from the relatively calm 2010–2019 period, rather than using the large 2021–2022 misses as a permissive benchmark. Make that comparison operational by fixing forecast horizons, outcome definitions, aggregation, data vintages, and scoring measures in advance. Specify acceptable interval coverage and width so that broad uncertainty bands cannot substitute for informative prediction. The historical benchmark is a proposed reference whose comparability must be justified.
completion_criteria.label: Forecast accuracy meets pre-registered 2010–2019 benchmarks with informative intervals

completion_criteria.text: Pre-specify how subsequent shocks, policy deviations, and revisions to economic data will be handled. Conditional forecasts must state their assumptions clearly, and evaluation must distinguish errors in those conditions from errors in the model's predicted response. An ex post decomposition made after the inflation path is known would not satisfy this prospective demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective evaluation separates conditioning errors from predicted-response errors

completion_criteria.text: For reproducibility, independent researchers should be able to reconstruct the committed forecasts and scores from archived code, model specifications, parameter estimates, data vintages, and computational settings. Supporting identification evidence should explain why the proposed primitives can be treated as stable over the policies being compared. These are proposed requirements for a convincing demonstration, not claims that a standard protocol already exists.
completion_criteria.label: Independent researchers reconstruct committed forecasts and scores from archives

completion_criteria.text: Passing one transition would establish performance within that tested setting. Broader confidence would require additional prospective transitions and identification evidence relevant to alternative rules, with explicit boundaries for countries, institutions, shock sizes, and policy changes. A finite series of successes would demonstrate breadth, not literal universality, and would not automatically validate every unobserved policy alternative.
completion_criteria.label: Additional prospective transitions demonstrate breadth within explicit applicability boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: ECO-02, Prospective transport of causal policy effects across populations, shares the demand for predictions that survive a change in context. The intended distinction is that ECO-02 transports a program effect to another population while holding the regime fixed, whereas ECO-08 concerns behavior changing with the monetary or fiscal rule itself. Full specifications of ECO-02 were not supplied, so this is an intended boundary rather than a verified exhaustive separation.

Roster-based comparison: ECO-10, Liquidity and credit without run-prone debt, concerns the design of financial arrangements that avoid runs. ECO-08 concerns evaluating macroeconomic consequences under alternative policy regimes. Such financial arrangements could become an application for regime evaluation, but crisis-resistant financial design and credible structural counterfactuals remain distinct capabilities. Only ECO-10's title and the research's brief scope description were supplied.

Roster-based comparison: ECO-01, Empirically valid aggregate market laws beyond the Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu barrier, addresses reliable aggregate relationships, while ECO-03, A predictive and welfare-coherent theory of boundedly rational choice, addresses individual choice. Either could inform the mechanisms or expectation responses used in ECO-08. Neither title alone implies a model validated across policy regimes. The computational paper illustrates the distinction between a method for finding an equilibrium and an empirical account of how people form expectations.

Roster-based comparison: ECO-07, A verified, manipulable law of sustained productivity growth, shares an ambition to support interventions with reliable causal knowledge, but targets sustained growth rather than macroeconomic regime transitions. ECO-04, An interpersonally comparable, preference-respecting measure of welfare, would address how outcomes are valued; ECO-08 addresses their predicted consequences. Forecasting inflation and employment does not itself settle welfare comparisons.

Roster-based comparison: ECO-05 concerns voluntary provision of global public goods, ECO-06 household markets for income risk, and ECO-09 allocation under private information. These could supply institutions or interventions whose macroeconomic consequences merit evaluation. Their titles identify separate design problems, however, and the supplied record provides no basis for treating their solutions as either sufficient or necessary for ECO-08.

change_log.change: Replaced invariance of all model parameters with the distinction between stable primitives and policy-dependent decision rules.
change_log.reason: This preserves Lucas's scientific distinction and avoids requiring behavioral coefficients to remain fixed when policy changes.

change_log.change: Recast present-day unavailability as an unresolved field-status question.
change_log.reason: The historical critique and one computational paper, without freshness-search results, cannot establish field-wide absence through November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Preserved the large-shock price-setting claim as an explicitly unverified consideration.
change_log.reason: No retained source supports the assertion, but that gap does not invalidate the concept or justify presenting the claim as disproved.

change_log.change: Retained the IMF forecast-error figures and Bernanke–Blanchard interpretation with explicit attribution and access qualifications.
change_log.reason: Their explanatory and quantitative detail is useful, but the review lacked source artifacts needed to verify it.

change_log.change: Added exact solver runtimes, hardware, averaging scope, equilibrium assumptions, preliminary date, and extraction limitations.
change_log.reason: These details substantiate computational progress while limiting conclusions to the demonstrated benchmarks.

change_log.change: Acknowledged the solver authors' theoretical Lucas-critique claim without treating it as empirical validation.
change_log.reason: The review identifies the claim as relevant, while distinguishing it from identified invariant primitives and real-world prospective performance.

change_log.change: Removed the conclusion that computation is no longer a gap and qualified the engineering analogy.
change_log.reason: Fast benchmark solutions do not eliminate general computational barriers, and one successful transition does not establish counterfactual validity or reliable control.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed prospective protocol with information timing, comparable scoring, interval informativeness, reproducibility, and treatment of shocks and policy deviations.
change_log.reason: These additions make the demonstration assessable while preserving its status as a proposal.

change_log.change: Separated related concepts using the supplied roster and qualified comparisons based only on titles or brief descriptions.
change_log.reason: This preserves distinct entries without implying that their full specifications were available.

unresolved_issues: The exact IMF forecast-error statistics and Bernanke–Blanchard decomposition remain unverified within the supplied review because no source artifacts were captured.
No retained evidence establishes whether large shocks change price-setting frequencies in the manner asserted by the original research.
The supplied record cannot determine the field-wide availability of prospectively validated structural regime counterfactuals as of November 1, 2026.

The computational paper's separately mentioned August 2026 version date is not substantiated by the retained December 2025 version-1 materials; its truncated PDF extraction also limits assessment of the complete paper.
The referenced reviewed-and-not-added note was not supplied and cannot resolve any computational or evidence question.
The proposed test still requires concrete choices of transition, outcomes, scoring thresholds, comparable historical forecasts, and identification evidence; none is an established universal standard.
Full definitions of neighboring roster concepts were not supplied, so their precise boundaries and overlaps remain provisional.

brief.title: Predicting what new economic policy rules would do
possible: Before changing how interest rates, taxes or spending respond to economic conditions, policymakers could compare the likely effects on prices, jobs and production. The model would account for people and businesses changing their plans when they learn that the rules have changed.
why: Central banks and treasuries would have a stronger basis for choosing policy rules before adopting them. They could compare tradeoffs between controlling inflation and supporting economic activity, prepare for transitions, and explain the uncertainty surrounding their choices.

sources.showed: Lucas explained why successful short-term forecasts do not establish that a model can compare policy rules. People change their decisions when the policy process changes.
sources.quote:
simulations using these models can, in principle, provide no 
useful information as to the actual consequences of alteruative economic policies.
sources.cited_for: Policy comparisons must account for changes in people's expectations and choices.
sources.not_established: The critique does not establish that every later model fails to handle policy changes.

sources.showed: This is an analysis of inflation forecast errors following the pandemic.
sources.cited_for: The pandemic inflation surge provides a stress test for economic forecasting.
sources.not_established: Forecast misses alone do not show that failing to model a change in policy rules caused the errors.

sources.showed: This is an explanation of US pandemic-era inflation that separates price shocks from labor-market pressures.
sources.cited_for: Explaining inflation after it happens is different from predicting it before a policy transition.
sources.not_established: An explanation fitted after events does not establish forecasting performance through a future policy change.

sources.who: Yucheng Yang, Chiyuan Wang, Andreas Schaab and Benjamin Moll
sources.showed: In a preliminary paper, the authors solved benchmark economic models with differing households in minutes. Their method restricts the information households use to make decisions.
sources.quote:
We illustrate the approach in the Krusell-Smith model, the Huggett model with
aggregate shocks, and a HANK model with a forward-looking Phillips curve, all of which
we solve globally within minutes.
sources.cited_for: Faster computation can help make demanding economic models practical to explore.
sources.not_established: Fast benchmark calculations do not establish realistic human learning or accurate forecasts through actual policy changes.

shown: Lucas established the conceptual obstacle: relationships that help forecast an economy under existing policy can change when the rules change.
Yang and colleagues have demonstrated fast calculations for benchmark models. This is computational progress; it does not demonstrate reliable comparisons of real policy alternatives.
missing: A convincing demonstration would need evidence of economic mechanisms that remain stable across the policy rules being compared.
Forecasts committed before actual policy transitions would need to predict how expectations, inflation and economic activity adjust.
Successful forecasts would need complementary evidence that the model can assess alternatives that were never implemented.

milestones.label: Forecasts committed before a policy change
milestones.explanation: A model, forecasts, uncertainty ranges and scoring rules would have to be fixed before a defined transition, then evaluated over two years. This would test predictions made before outcomes were known.

milestones.label: Accurate forecasts with useful uncertainty ranges
milestones.explanation: Errors would have to meet a predefined benchmark from the calm historical period, with uncertainty ranges narrow enough to inform decisions. This would prevent vague predictions from counting as success.

milestones.label: Forecast errors separated by cause
milestones.explanation: Evaluation would have to distinguish wrong assumptions about shocks or policy from wrong predictions of the economy's response, using rules fixed beforehand. This would clarify what the test says about the model.

milestones.label: Independent reconstruction of forecasts and scores
milestones.explanation: Independent researchers would have to reproduce forecasts and scores from archived materials, alongside evidence for stable underlying mechanisms. This would make the result reproducible and its policy comparisons assessable.

milestones.label: Success across further policy transitions
milestones.explanation: Further forecasts made before transitions would have to succeed, with evidence supporting comparisons across explicitly bounded settings. This would establish breadth beyond the initial case.

uncertain: The proposed historical benchmark needs a justified comparison, including agreed outcomes, forecast horizons and scoring thresholds.
Success through a realized transition does not settle whether predictions for policies never adopted are correct.
The boundaries of success across countries, institutions, shock sizes and policy changes remain to be established.

page.title: Structural policy evaluation across macroeconomic regimes
page.definition: A structural macroeconomic model estimates inflation, employment and output under alternative monetary or fiscal rules, meaning policies that specify responses to economic conditions. Its estimates account for changes in private expectations and decisions, with empirical evidence supporting the mechanisms assumed stable across those rules.

goal.need: In an IMF working paper’s panel of 54 economies, 21 had significantly positive coefficients in tests for sluggish updating of inflation forecasts over the first quarter of 2011 to the third quarter of 2022. These results motivate evaluation of models used to inform policy; they do not identify policy-regime misspecification as the cause.

figures.caption: Reported world-average annual headline-inflation forecast misses
figures.note: Figure 2 reports purchasing-power-parity GDP-weighted averages using January WEO forecasts. The 2022 value is an October-minus-January forecast revision, rather than an error against realised annual inflation. The figure does not state the country count underlying these aggregates.

statements.quote: choosing the best policy strategy requires comparing the likely economic outcomes under alternative policies
statements.context: The independent review commissioned by the Bank’s Court was published on 12 April 2024; this passage concerns monetary policy.

completion.title: Independent prospective replication confirms a model’s policy-regime predictions.
completion.criterion: In at least two policy-rule transitions within a declared domain, the same structural framework predicts inflation, employment and output, including expectation adjustment. Parameters and joint predictive distributions under the old and new rules are fixed before each announcement. Over each evaluation window fixed in advance, the new-rule distribution gives the observed outcomes strictly higher cumulative log predictive density than the unchanged-rule benchmark, using identical nonpolicy shock assumptions. Identification and intervention-specific invariance evidence support the mechanisms retained. An independent team conducts the second prospective test and reproduces the first.
completion.set_by: Atlas; proposed scoped demonstration, because no external end-to-end acceptance standard was located.
completion.basis: Searched Federal Reserve policy-rule guidance, Bank of England forecasting reviews and research agendas, and econometric identification/invariance papers; no end-to-end acceptance standard was found. McKay and Wolf already identify rule counterfactuals under explicit model assumptions. This Atlas test adds prospective replication; its log-score comparison and two-transition minimum are Atlas choices. Passing supports a declared domain and does not directly validate policies never implemented.

milestones.title: A structural model computes outcomes under alternative rules with endogenous expectations.
milestones.criterion: Solve a structural model under alternative policy rules, recomputing private decisions and expectations. Leeper and Zha (2003) demonstrate a two-regime laboratory model with Bayesian updating. Separately, Yang et al.’s preprint submitted on 21 December 2025 reports mean runtimes of 56.55, 75.29 and 199.53 seconds for three heterogeneous-agent benchmarks, with 10 runs each on one NVIDIA A100 GPU. These are restricted-perceptions equilibria, not empirical validation.
milestones.set_by: Structural policy-evaluation convention formulated by Lucas (1976), section 6; this is a theoretical demonstration without a solver-speed threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: scientific quantitative policy evaluations available to us are comparisons of the consequences of alternative policy rules.

milestones.title: Policy-shock responses enforce a counterfactual rule in model paths and prior expectations.
milestones.criterion: In McKay and Wolf’s linear model class, policy affects private behaviour only through the current and expected future instrument path, and baseline and counterfactual equilibria are unique. Identified contemporaneous and news-shock responses must enforce the alternative rule at every horizon, both along the outcome path and in prior expectations. Their empirical application combines two US monetary-shock series and approximates several rule counterfactuals; exact identification under assumptions does not establish exact empirical recovery.
milestones.set_by: Published econometric identification criterion of McKay and Wolf (2023), Proposition 1; restricted to their stated model class, with monetary-policy empirical applications.
milestones.threshold_quote: All that is required is that those policy shocks imply the same expected instrument path from date-0 onwards as the counterfactual rule.

milestones.title: A model survives empirical tests of the invariance needed for its policy comparisons.
milestones.criterion: Across observed changes in policy-generating processes, data do not reject the specified invariance restrictions on the mechanisms retained for policy comparison; decision rules may change. The relevant alternatives, test size and power must be established. Engle and Hendry report F(5,60)=0.85 for five superexogeneity test terms in a UK money-demand equation, using 71 quarters from the second quarter of 1965 through the fourth quarter of 1982. This is component evidence, not a full-model pass; non-rejection does not prove invariance.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; no model-wide invariance acceptance criterion was found in the econometric papers and central-bank reviews searched. Engle and Hendry supply a published component test.

milestones.title: A model beats its unchanged-rule benchmark prospectively through one policy-rule change.
milestones.criterion: Before one policy-rule announcement, fix the model, parameters and joint predictive distributions of inflation, employment and output under the old and new rules. Over a window fixed in advance, the new-rule prediction has strictly greater cumulative log predictive density for the observed outcomes than the unchanged-rule benchmark, with identical nonpolicy shock assumptions and data vintages. Expectation adjustment must be modelled. This is the first prospective pass required by completion; it does not itself validate the unobserved old-rule outcome.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; no common prospective regime-change forecast benchmark, evaluation horizon or acceptance threshold was found in the central-bank reviews searched.

not_found: No external end-to-end acceptance standard or complete milestone ladder was located in the central-bank and econometric sources searched.
No independently replicated prospective demonstration meeting the stated completion criterion was located.
The supplied Lucas and IMF eLibrary links and the supplied SSRN page could not be retrieved; alternate Lucas and IMF copies were accessible.
